newsitem.title: USA: Republicans pour in cash to retain Congress.
newsitem.headline: Republicans pour in cash to retain Congress.

text.p: Republicans are pouring money into a handful of close Senate races and dozens of tight House of Representatives contests trying to turn back a Democratic tide that threatens to end their rule in Congress after only two years.

Republicans reported that on Monday of this week alone they spent close to $1 million in a few select Senate races, exploiting a summer Supreme Court decision that blew a giant hole in campaign spending limits.

Democrats need a net gain of three seats to split the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. Assuming President Clinton wins re-election, Vice President Al Gore could cast a vote to break ties and give Democrats control.
Democrats need a gain of 18 seats to take control of the 435-member House. Republicans now hold a 235-198 advantage, with one independent who generally votes with the Democrats and one seat vacant.

The big question, according to political analysts, is whether voters would prefer divided government by re-electing Democrat President Bill Clinton and giving him a Republican Congress as a counterbalance? Or could Democrats sweep back into control of Congress on Clinton's coattails?

"The whole business of coattails I think is just garbage," said political analyst Charles Cook, noting that since the second World War no full-term presidential re-election landslide brought significant Congressional gains.
But California Republican political consultant Allan Hoffenblum disagrees.

"We haven't gone through a full-term Democrat being re-elected by a wide margin since World War II," he said. "We know millions will vote for a Republican for president and a Democrat for Congress, but what happens when they vote Democrat for president? All we can do is guess."
Experts said the outcome of the electoral war could turn on money and regional differences in voting patterns.

According to an official report to the Federal Election Commission, the National Republican Senatorial Committee's independent expenditure unit spent $830,000 on Senate races on Monday alone and a further $806,000 last Thursday, another high-spending day.

The Monday spending included $164,000 in Kansas to help Republican Representative Sam Brownback defeat Jill Docking for the seat Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole resigned, and $318,000 in New Hampshire to run negative ads against Dick Swett, who has mounted an unexpectedly strong challenge against Republican Senator Bob Smith. Democrats lack the money to make any comparable expenditures.
At most, 16 of the 34 seats at stake in the Senate are close, which permits this kind of spending assault.

In races for the House, Republicans say they are spending $26 million to help their candidates. But they face trouble in protecting House freshmen who were the strongest allies of the highly unpopular House Speaker, Newt Gingrich.

A Chicago Tribune poll on Wednesday backed what analysts had said for months: Republican Representative Michael Flanagan is likely to lose the solidly Democratic district he won from indicted veteran Dan Rostenkowski in 1994.
When Republicans took over the House for the first time in 40 years in 1994, they made their greatest gains in the Pacific Northwest. Now they could face losses there.

"Republicans by and large are on the defence," said Tim Hibbits, an independent pollster in Portland, Oregon. "They're going to take losses" in Oregon, Washington and Idaho, where Republicans now hold an overall 11-5 advantage in the House and a 4-2 advantage in the Senate, he said.
Hibbits predicted Republicans will lose two to seven House seats in that region.

The best hope for Republicans is in the conservative South, where they hope the steady march from Democrat to Republican in the last few decades continues this year. Political analyst Cook predicts Republicans could gain five to eight net seats in the House from that region.

The wild card may be California, which has a trove of 52 House seats split evenly between the parties. Hoffenblum, who edits the bipartisan California Target Book in Los Angeles which assesses state races, said Democrats may lose two seats or win as many as four.
Republican freshmen are under siege in California. In the northern part of the state, Michela Alioto is running neck-and-neck with freshman Republican Frank Riggs.
Near San Diego on the Mexican border, college professor Peter Navarro is neck-and-neck with freshman Brian Bilbray.
